name: Nasrin Sotoudeh
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; completed master's in international law in 1989 (age ~26) but passed the bar exam only in 1995 (age 32) and received her law license in 2003 (age 40). Major human rights activism began after 2009.
early_history_summary: Born into a religious middle-class family in Tehran, Sotoudeh earned a master's degree in international law from Shahid Beheshti University in 1989. She passed the Iranian bar exam in 1995 but was blocked from practicing law for eight years by the Ministry of Intelligence, working as a journalist in the interim.
family_context_summary: Born to a religious middle-class family in Tehran; father was a businessman and mother a homemaker.
evidence_summary: Sotoudeh's early career was marked by institutional barriers: she passed the bar exam in 1995 but could not practice law until 2003. Her major human rights work began after the 2009 Iranian elections. No material milestone by age 26 is documented.

name: Joaquín Sabina
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; published in literary magazine Poesía 70 in 1970 (age 21) but first book 'Memoria del exilio' appeared in 1976 (age 27) and first album 'Inventario' in 1978 (age 29). Fame arrived in the 1980s.
early_history_summary: Born in Úbeda, Spain, Sabina began writing poetry at 14 and played in a teenage rockabilly band. He studied philology at the University of Granada, collaborated with the magazine Poesía 70 in 1970, and then went into exile in London using a fake passport, where he wrote his first songs.
family_context_summary: Born in Úbeda, Jaén; father was a police inspector and mother a housewife. Family was very Catholic.
evidence_summary: Sabina started writing poetry at 14 and was in a band as a teenager, but his first published book came at 27 and first album at 29. His collaboration with Poesía 70 magazine at 21 was notable but not a material career milestone. Widespread fame came in the 1980s.

name: Tibor Klampár
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Championship gold medal in men's doubles with István Jónyer at the 1971 World Table Tennis Championships in Nagoya at age 17, defeating the Chinese pair Chuang Tse-tung and Liang Ko-liang in the final.
early_history_summary: Born in Budapest, Klampár started table tennis at age 8 in 1961, initially rejected by a coach at Vörös Meteor but transferred to Postás SE where his older brother Józsi effectively trained him. He won the European Youth Championship at 13, became Hungarian national champion from 1969 (age 16), and debuted for the Hungarian national team in 1968 at age 15.
family_context_summary: Born in Budapest; his two older sisters were NB I (first division) table tennis players, which led him to the sport. His older brother Józsi became his de facto coach despite having no formal coaching qualifications.
primary_early_advantage_tags: sibling-coach,early specialization,Hungarian table tennis pipeline,youth champion
evidence_summary: Klampár began table tennis at age 8, guided by his older brother Józsi who provided intense daily training at Postás SE in Budapest. His two older sisters were first-division players, giving him family-domain exposure. He won the European Youth Championship at 13, became Hungarian champion at 16, and won World Championship gold in doubles at 17. The Hungarian table tennis system provided a strong elite performance pipeline during this era.
starting_point: Born in Budapest in 1953; two older sisters were first-division table tennis players, and his older brother Józsi became his de facto coach, transferring him between clubs.
current_position: Retired former international table tennis player; 2-time World champion, 3-time European champion, 1981 World Cup winner; inducted into European Table Tennis Hall of Fame in 2015.

trajectory.event: Won the European Youth Championship in table tennis.
Became Hungarian national table tennis champion for the first time.
Won World Championship gold in men's doubles with István Jónyer at the Nagoya World Table Tennis Championships.
Won World Championship team gold at the Pyongyang World Table Tennis Championships.
Won the Table Tennis World Cup singles title in Kuala Lumpur and the Europe Top-16 tournament.
Finished fourth in men's singles at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, table tennis's Olympic debut.
Inducted into the European Table Tennis Hall of Fame.

name: César Luis Menotti
milestone_by_age_26: Debuted in the Argentine Primera División for Rosario Central on July 31, 1960 at age 21, scoring a goal in a 3-1 victory over Boca Juniors; later represented Argentina at the 1963 Copa América (third place) and won the Argentine Primera División with Boca Juniors in 1965.
early_history_summary: Born in Rosario, Argentina, Menotti grew up in a football-loving family; his father Antonio had played for Rosario Central in the amateur era. After his father's death in 1955, economic hardship pushed Menotti toward professional football. He played in the Carcarañense League for pay before being scouted by Rosario Central, where he debuted in Primera División in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in Rosario; father Antonio Menotti played for Rosario Central in the amateur era (one official match in 1926) and was a passionate fan. Father died of cancer in 1955 when Menotti was 16, plunging the family into economic crisis.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a former Rosario Central player and passionate football fan who initially resisted Menotti pursuing professional football, preferring he focus on studies. Father's football connection provided early exposure to the sport.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father's death,economic hardship,football culture,Rosario,early professional debut
evidence_summary: Menotti grew up in Rosario immersed in football culture through his father, a former Rosario Central player. His father's death in 1955 created economic hardship that pushed him toward professional football, playing for pay in the Carcarañense League. He debuted in Primera División at 21, played for Argentina at the 1963 Copa América, and later played for Boca Juniors and Santos alongside Pelé. His tall, athletic frame (1.93m) and natural ability facilitated his early rise.
starting_point: Born in Rosario, Argentina in 1938; father was a former Rosario Central player who died when Menotti was 16, pushing the family into economic hardship.
current_position: Died May 5, 2024 at age 85 in Buenos Aires; final role: manager of the Argentina national team (2018-2023). Best known as the coach who won the 1978 FIFA World Cup with Argentina.

trajectory.event: Debuted in Argentine Primera División for Rosario Central, scoring in a 3-1 win over Boca Juniors.
Represented Argentina at the 1963 Copa América, finishing in third place.
Won the Argentine Primera División with Boca Juniors.
Played for Santos FC alongside Pelé, winning the Campeonato Brasileiro Série A.
Led Huracán to the Argentine Metropolitano championship as manager, establishing his coaching reputation.
Won the 1978 FIFA World Cup as head coach of the Argentina national team.
Died on May 5, 2024 in Buenos Aires after a long illness.

name: Armin Hary
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold in the 100m and 4x100m relay at the 1958 European Athletics Championships in Stockholm at age 21, establishing himself as one of the world's top sprinters.
early_history_summary: Born in Gersweiler, Saarland, Hary played soccer throughout childhood before switching to sprinting at age 14. He was largely self-coached, famously dispensing with a coach. Within four years of starting sprint training, he won the European Championships in 1958, becoming the first German to win the 100m at a major international championship.
family_context_summary: Son of a Saarland coal miner who was also a German wrestling champion. Grew up in working-class conditions in the Saarland region.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a coal miner and German wrestling champion, suggesting an athletic family background, though not directly in sprinting.
evidence_summary: Hary possessed extraordinary physical gifts, particularly his reaction time of 0.04 seconds (vs. 0.132 average), which earned him the nickname 'Thief of Starts.' His father was a coal miner and wrestling champion, suggesting inherited athletic ability. Hary started sprinting at 14, was self-coached, and won the European Championships at 21. He came from a working-class Saarland background with no documented financial support or elite training infrastructure.
starting_point: Born in Gersweiler, Saarland in 1937; son of a coal miner and German wrestling champion. Grew up in working-class conditions.
current_position: Retired sprinter living in Germany; last known public recognition was induction into the German Sports Hall of Fame in 2011. Previously worked as a real estate trader.

trajectory.event: Won gold in the 100m and 4x100m relay at the European Athletics Championships in Stockholm.
Became the first man to run 100m in 10.0 seconds, setting a world record in Zurich on June 21.
Won Olympic gold in the 100m at the 1960 Rome Olympics, becoming the first non-American to win the event since 1928.
Suspended by the German athletics federation for padding expense reports and dual sponsorship deals; subsequently retired due to car accident injuries.
Selected as Germany's Runner of the Millennium.
Inducted into the German Sports Hall of Fame.

name: Herta Müller
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; first book 'Niederungen' was published in 1982 (age 29). She was associated with the Aktionsgruppe Banat literary circle during university (1973-1976) and worked as a factory translator until 1979, but had no published work or major recognition by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in 1953 in Nițchidorf, a German-speaking village in Romania, Müller studied German and Romanian literature at the University of Timișoara from 1973 to 1976. She joined the Aktionsgruppe Banat literary circle opposed to Ceaușescu's dictatorship, then worked as a translator at a machine factory until dismissed in 1979 for refusing to inform for the Securitate.
family_context_summary: Born to Banat Swabian Catholic farmers in Nițchidorf, Romania. Father served in the Waffen SS during WWII and worked as a truck driver. Mother was deported to a Soviet forced labor camp from 1945-1950. Grandfather's property was confiscated by the Communist regime.
evidence_summary: Müller's early life was shaped by the oppression of the Romanian Communist regime and her German-speaking minority background. She joined a dissident literary circle at university but had no published work until age 29. The Securitate's harassment and her dismissal from work created adversity but did not produce a material milestone by age 26.

name: Jiří Kylián
milestone_by_age_26: Made his choreographic debut with 'Paradox' for the Stuttgart Ballet's Noverre Society in 1970 at age 23, a piece he choreographed, composed music for, and performed; it was praised by John Cranko and Margot Fonteyn, who invited it to London.
early_history_summary: Born in Prague in 1947, Kylián began ballet training at the School of the National Ballet Prague at age 9, inspired initially by circus acrobatics. He entered the Prague Conservatory in 1962, where mentor Zora Šemberová shaped his development. In 1967 he received a scholarship to the Royal Ballet School in London, where he met John Cranko, who recruited him to the Stuttgart Ballet in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Prague; father Václav was a banker who rose from a simple village background to become director of the largest savings bank in Czechoslovakia. Mother Markéta was a dancer-child prodigy who sold out theaters at age 10.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was a child prodigy dancer, providing direct domain exposure and family support for pursuing dance. Father's banking career provided middle-class stability.
primary_early_advantage_tags: dancer mother,Prague Conservatory,Zora Šemberová mentor,John Cranko,Stuttgart Ballet,Royal Ballet School scholarship
evidence_summary: Kylián benefited from a strong family-domain connection through his dancer-prodigy mother and banker father, who supported his early ballet training from age 9. The Prague Conservatory provided elite training under mentor Zora Šemberová. A scholarship to the Royal Ballet School in London connected him to John Cranko, who recruited him to the Stuttgart Ballet at 21. His choreographic debut at 23 was praised by Cranko and Margot Fonteyn, launching his choreographic career.
starting_point: Born in Prague in 1947; father was a banker who became director of the largest savings bank in Czechoslovakia, mother was a dancer-child prodigy who sold out theaters at age 10.
current_position: Retired choreographer living in The Hague area, Netherlands; former artistic director of Nederlands Dans Theater (1975-1999). Received the Order of the White Lion from Czech Republic in 2024, the country's highest honor.

trajectory.event: Admitted to the Prague Conservatory, where he studied under mentor Zora Šemberová and created his first student choreographies.
Received a scholarship to study at the Royal Ballet School in London, where he met choreographer John Cranko.
Joined the Stuttgart Ballet under John Cranko, fleeing Prague during the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.
Made choreographic debut with 'Paradox' for the Stuttgart Ballet's Noverre Society, praised by Cranko and Margot Fonteyn.
Became artistic director of Nederlands Dans Theater in The Hague, jointly with Hans Knill.
Put NDT on the international map with 'Sinfonietta' at the Charleston Festival; founded NDT2 for young dancers.
Stepped down as artistic director of NDT after 24 years, remaining as house choreographer.
Decorated with the Order of the White Lion, the Czech Republic's highest honor, by President Petr Pavel.

name: Anders Nordström
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; trained as a physician at Karolinska Institutet, but his international health career (Swedish Red Cross, Sida, WHO) developed in the 1990s and 2000s. Acting Director-General of WHO in 2006.
early_history_summary: Born in Sweden in 1960, Nordström trained as a physician at the Karolinska Institutet. His early career involved work with the Swedish Red Cross in Cambodia and the ICRC in Iran, but these assignments appear to have occurred after age 26. His major roles at Sida, the Global Fund, and WHO came in the 2000s.
evidence_summary: Nordström's career in international health policy developed gradually after medical training at Karolinska Institutet. No specific dated milestone by age 26 could be identified. His significant roles at the Global Fund (2002), WHO (2003-2007), and Sida (2008-2010) came well into his 40s.

name: Manuel Rivera-Ortiz
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; graduated cum laude with a BA in English from Nazareth College in 1995 (age 27) and received his Master's from Columbia Journalism School in 1998 (age 30). First photography award (En Foco New Works) came in 2004 (age 36).
early_history_summary: Born into a poor family in Guayama, Puerto Rico, Rivera-Ortiz grew up in a tin shack without running water. His father was a sugar cane cutter and migrant farmworker. The family moved to Holyoke, Massachusetts when he was 11, where he took his first photography courses in a summer migrant education program. He later moved to Rochester, NY, worked as a journalist, and graduated from Nazareth College in 1995.
family_context_summary: Born into extreme poverty in Guayama, Puerto Rico; father was a sugar cane cutter and migrant farmworker, mother a homemaker. Grew up in a corrugated tin shack with dirt floors, no running water. Parents separated when he was 11; father moved the children to the US mainland.
evidence_summary: Rivera-Ortiz grew up in extreme poverty in Puerto Rico, moving to the US mainland at age 11. He took his first photography courses in a summer migrant education program but did not pursue photography professionally until well after college. His BA was completed at 27 and his first photography award came at 36. No material milestone by age 26 is documented.

name: Vladimir Aksyonov
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Aksyonov graduated from the 10th Military Aviation School in 1955 (age 20) and was working as an engineer at Korolev OKB, but was not selected as a cosmonaut until 1973 (age 38). First spaceflight was Soyuz 22 in 1976 (age 41).
early_history_summary: Born in Giblitsy, Ryazan Oblast, Aksyonov was orphaned in his youth; his father was killed in WWII in 1944 and his mother died in 1949. Raised by maternal grandparents, he attended Mytishchi Engineering College (graduated 1953) and the 10th Military Aviation School for Primary Pilot Training (graduated 1955 with honors). He then worked as an engineer before being selected for cosmonaut training in 1973.
family_context_summary: Orphaned young; father killed in action on the Eastern Front in 1944, mother died in 1949. Raised by maternal grandparents who were well educated.
evidence_summary: Aksyonov was orphaned as a teenager and raised by his grandparents. He completed engineering and aviation training by age 20 but worked as an engineer at Korolev OKB for many years before being selected as a cosmonaut at 38. His spaceflights came in his 40s. No material milestone by age 26 is documented.

name: Kenzō Takada
milestone_by_age_26: Won the prestigious Soen Prize for fashion design in 1960 at age 21, while a student at Bunka Fashion College in Tokyo, and began working as a designer for the Sanai department store creating up to 40 girls' clothing designs per month.
early_history_summary: Born in Himeji, Japan, Takada developed an interest in fashion from his sisters' magazines. He briefly studied literature at Kobe City University in 1957 but left after his father's death, enrolling at Bunka Fashion College in 1958 as one of its first male students. He won the Soen Prize in 1960, then worked for the Sanai department store before moving to Paris in 1964-1965.
family_context_summary: Born in Himeji to parents who ran a hotel (innkeepers). One of seven children. Father died during Takada's first year at university. Family did not approve of a fashion career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were innkeepers with no apparent fashion industry connection.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bunka Fashion College,Soen Prize,Sanai department store,first male student,Paris fashion scene
evidence_summary: Takada enrolled at Bunka Fashion College in 1958 as one of the first male students, giving him access to a prestigious fashion education pipeline. He won the Soen Prize at 21, recognized as an emerging designer of distinction, and immediately began professional work at the Sanai department store designing up to 40 outfits monthly. His father's death and family disapproval of fashion created adversity but also freed him to pursue his chosen path. Bunka's cohort included future design stars Junko Koshino and Mitsuhiro Matsuda.
starting_point: Born in Himeji, Japan in 1939 to innkeeper parents; one of seven children. Father died during Takada's first year at university, after which he left to pursue fashion against family wishes.
current_position: Died October 4, 2020 in Paris at age 81 from COVID-19 complications. Final status: retired from his eponymous brand Kenzo (left in 1999); brand acquired by LVMH in 1993.

trajectory.event: Enrolled at Bunka Fashion College in Tokyo as one of the first male students, against his family's wishes.
Won the prestigious Soen Prize for fashion design and began working as a designer for the Sanai department store.
Moved to Paris by boat, beginning his immersion in the French fashion world.
Opened his first shop 'Jungle Jap' in the Galerie Vivienne in Paris and staged his first fashion show; Elle featured one of his designs on its cover.
Launched the Kenzo brand officially with a flagship store on the Place des Victoires in Paris.
Sold the Kenzo brand to LVMH.
Left his namesake brand after his final show at the Zénith concert hall in Paris.
Died on October 4 in Paris from COVID-19 complications.

name: Katalin Karikó
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Karikó began her PhD in biochemistry at the University of Szeged around 1977 (age 22) working in Jenö Tomasz's RNA lab, but completed her PhD in 1982 (age 27). No published papers, patents, or major discoveries are documented before age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in 1955 in Kisújszállás, Hungary, Karikó grew up without running water or television. Her father was a butcher and her mother a bookkeeper. She developed an interest in biology through an excellent school teacher and attended the University of Szeged, where she began PhD research in RNA in 1977 under Jenö Tomasz, completing her doctorate in 1982.
family_context_summary: Born in Kisújszállás, a small town of 10,000 in Hungary; father was a butcher, mother a bookkeeper. Grew up in a very simple home without running water, television, or refrigerator.
evidence_summary: Karikó grew up in a small Hungarian town in modest circumstances, with a butcher father and bookkeeper mother. She entered the University of Szeged and began RNA research during her PhD, but her doctorate was completed at 27. Her groundbreaking work with Drew Weissman came in the mid-2000s, and the Nobel Prize in 2023. No material milestone by age 26 is documented.
